extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literature, philosophy, and aesthetics (interested in Plato and the theory of poetry)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria and evaluative principles about poetry, art, and fiction as discussed in a literary-philosophical analysis of Plato (and his critics). Useful for judging or composing poetry/fiction with reference to philosophical/aesthetic standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to universals vs particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets are concerned with the inferior faculties—the lower with particulars of sense—whereas philosophy deals with universals and abstractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Plato's principal critique: poetry belongs to the level of sense and particulars and so cannot reach the truth of universals. Contrast with Aristotle, who argues poetry is truer than history because it is concerned with universals. Use this criterion to judge whether a poem aims at particular sensory detail or at universal, abstract truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority and interpretability of poetic texts
rubrics_metrics.description: Homer and Hesiod 'could not be made a rule of life by any process of legitimate interpretation'; poets are not critics of their own writings and may be less able to interpret them than readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume poetic texts are straightforward moral or practical guides. The author warns against treating poets as authoritative ethical instructors; poets may be better read as expressive artists than rule-makers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as potential vehicle of falsehood and political corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets (like sophists and rhetoricians) are accused of feigning, of being 'false priests, false prophets, lying spirits', and of fostering support for tyranny by basking in patronage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the political/moral alignment of poetic work: whether it idealizes or rationalizes corrupt power, flatters tyrants, or otherwise serves propaganda. The anti-pattern is prostituting the Muse to praise tyranny or to promote false ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional excitation vs moral/ intellectual function
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato objects that poetry excites the emotions; the modern response is that emotions are not intrinsically bad and art's vocation is 'to present thought in the form of feeling', enlisting feelings on the side of reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether emotional impact serves reason and moral ends (inspiring courage, resignation, sense of infinity) rather than merely stirring unregulated passions. Moderate indulgence of emotion is preferable to suppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitative art as compromise between ideal truth and representation
rubrics_metrics.description: All imitative art is subject to limitations: 'Something of ideal truth is sacrificed for the sake of the representation, and something in the exactness of the representation is sacrificed to the ideal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize trade-offs in craft choices (realism vs idealization). Good criticism/creation attends to how the work balances fidelity to particulars with striving for ideal or symbolic truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works of art as intermediates between sense and ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Works of art 'have a permanent element; they idealize and detain the passing thought, and are the intermediates between sense and ideas.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work transcends ephemeral sensation to enshrine a more lasting, idealized insight—i.e., whether it 'detains' thought in a memorable form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/contextual place of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry's place varies by historical stage: in infancy of mankind poetry was 'the whole of literature'; in modern times it can be 'the shadow or echo of her former self'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a piece with awareness of its historical/cultural context and the shifting social functions of poetry; expect different standards and roles in different eras.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transferability of poetic effects to prose and rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'charms of poetry have been partly transferred to prose'; rhetoric can serve as the handmaiden of politics and law can substitute for old poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating genre boundaries, note that poetic effects—imagery, emotional force—can appear in prose; assess success of prose using criteria similar to poetry when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability to cultural and thematic exhaustion
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative power may weaken with cultural change (science, new facts), and recurring subjects (e.g., love) risk exhaustion after countless variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique freshness and necessity of theme and approach. A work repeating well-worn treatments of love or familiar motifs should be judged for innovation or insight rather than mere reiteration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of art to religion and philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Art cannot claim parity with philosophy or religion and may corrupt them; yet art can also be the expression of highest truth and purest sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether art in a work supports or undermines deeper philosophical or religious aims. Some traditions may reject external artistic forms; gauge sensitivity to such audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal poetry as service to knowledge and goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: There might be a poetry 'which would be the hymn of divine perfection... which would elicit the simple principles, or... the essential forms, of truth and justice... preserve all the good of each generation and leave the bad unsung... based... on a clear insight into the nature of man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a high ideal: judge whether poetry aspires to ennoble, to distill ethical or metaphysical essentials, to renew moral imagination—examples praised: Aeschylus, Sophocles, Milton, Wordsworth, Hebrew prophets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of love as an artistic motive
rubrics_metrics.description: The illusion of the feelings commonly called love has been the inspiring influence of modern poetry and romance and may still incentive great thoughts and heroic deeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether love in a work is used merely as sentimental routine or as a spur to higher thought and action; the latter is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist crude moralizing; preserve poetic autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may argue that 'moralizing in verse is not poetry'; poets may rebel against attempts to set limits to fancy even while philosophers ask how poesy may be devoted to the good of mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the demand for moral seriousness with respect for poetic freedom. Excessive didacticism is an anti-pattern; successful works integrate moral depth without sacrificing poetic form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verisimilitude through precise, 'touches of nature'
rubrics_metrics.description: Credibility in marvelous narratives is increased by 'touches of nature'—precise coincidences, measured timings, plausible details (e.g., Er's timing, Odysseus choosing last, souls' behaviors)—as Defoe might use to win credibility for marvels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For fiction, employ specific, believable details, careful coincidences and small realistic touches to make extraordinary events feel credible. This is a practical craft rule for achieving narrative probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between public purpose and imaginative expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato protests against degeneracy in poetry—'want of serious purpose in modern fiction', 'time-serving of preachers or public writers', and 'the readers become what they read and are injuriously affected by them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work pursues mere entertainment or fashion at the expense of seriousness and formative influence; consider ethical consequences of popular writing and whether it elevates or degrades readers.
